ports.name: Bodega Bay
ports.summary: Sheltered bay anchorage and village port, listed by NOAA among the regional doghole ports though it functioned mainly as a produce/potato and general-cargo port rather than a chute port. Its lumber significance is early: Capt. Stephen Smith erected California's first steam saw- and grist-mill near Bodega in 1843 and shipped lumber to San Francisco in his vessel Fayaway. The 1889 Coast Pilot describes Bodega Port village on the lagoon behind the sand spit, used by small schooners, with no chute; the harbor was protected N/W/E and open only past Bodega Rock.

ports.name: Duncan's Landing
ports.summary: Doghole cove on Duncan's Point used to tranship lumber from the Duncan brothers' mill on the lower Russian River (the river itself being unnavigable to lumber vessels). ports.name: Rule's Landing
ports.summary: Wire-chute-only landing under Rule's Head, 1.5 mi NW of the Russian River mouth, on the Rule family ranch (John and Elizabeth Rule, land bought 1870). The 1889 Coast Pilot: 'located in 1877, but has since been abandoned'; a wire cable ran 150 yards from the bluff to a rock, vessels mooring beneath; the cable was taken down in 1884 and the business moved to Russian Gulch Landing. Douglass (1995) recorded railroad ties, a possible turntable, and frayed wire cable; the cove was the Russians' 'harbor sheltered for baidarkas.'

ports.name: Russian Gulch Landing (Sonoma)
ports.summary: Landing at the only sand-beach gulch north of the Russian River; vessels entered a 100-yard rock passage to load at a short, very steep chute built from the southeast point (1889 Coast Pilot; 11 ft at the chute end, 2 mooring buoys). It received Rule's Landing's business in 1884 and was supplied by steam railroad from the Russian River mills; after 1900 the Western Redwood Lumber Company operated a wire chute and storage yard here (c.1904 photo). Archaeology (2016) found railroad ties, roadbeds and buried wire cable.

ports.name: Fort Ross Cove
ports.summary: Russian-era prehistory in one line: the Russians maintained a small wharf and shipyard here, where shipwright Vasily Grudinin built the first ships constructed in California — brigs Rumiantsev (1818), Buldakov (1820), Volga (1822), Kiakhta (1824). American era: James W. Dixon built a 180-ft trough chute with 100-ft swing apron on the north bank in 1867 (used to c.1900); William Benitz had built a stone wharf pre-1870s, expanded by George W. Call in the 1870s with warehouse and derrick (destroyed 1901 when the schooner J. Eppinger wrecked into it); a wire chute operated c.1901-1920/21, rebuilt 1910, then dismantled and its machinery moved to Timber Cove. Vessels loaded lumber, cordwood, tanbark, stone, hides, produce and passengers; a railway was cut into the cliff's northern rim from blufftop to wharf.

ports.name: Timber Cove
ports.summary: Settlement from c.1856 with hotel, store and post office supporting a trough chute 'built sometime that decade,' the first such apparatus in the area (NOAA). George Weber and D.L.B. Ross built a mill 1.5 mi inland in 1861 (lasted 3 years); William R. Miller's sawmill ran from 1867 and had largely stripped the nearby hills by the 1870s. 481 schooner cargoes were transhipped 1868-74; the 1889 Coast Pilot shows the single trough chute (out to 16 ft of water, 5 mooring lines, 2 buoys) loading cordwood, posts, ties, tanbark and produce. Ernest Saltzig installed a wire chute in 1921 (transplanted from Fort Ross); lumber shipping ended by 1925.

ports.name: Stillwater Cove
ports.summary: Very small but sheltered cove usable year-round. Christian Friedrich Ruoff settled by fall 1851; after his 1854 death his widow Francesca ran the property and built a lumber chute by the late 1860s ('owned by Mrs. Ruoff in 1880'). The single chute on the NW side ran from the cliff past the outer rocks into 11 ft of water; vessels lay broadside with six mooring lines (1889 Coast Pilot); 249 wood loads shipped 1868-74. No town ever formed; no photos or drawings of the chute have been found, but rebates, ring bolts, pins and wire rope survive.

ports.name: Salt Point / Gerstle Cove
ports.summary: Joshua Hendy and Samuel Duncan brought the township's first steam sawmill here in 1853 (Hendy sold to Alex Duncan 1855; Duncan Bros. to 1860, ~30 million ft cut); the Duncans also quarried marine-terrace sandstone shipped to San Francisco and Mare Island. Before the 1870s cargo was lowered to ships on cables anchored to the cliffs; William R. Miller built a chute in 1872 and Funcke & Wasserman a second (public landing, 1876); by 1889 only the rebuilt inner chute remained (out to 13 ft of water, six mooring lines, two 80-ton vessels able to lie in the cove), abandoned by 1917. A horse-drawn wooden-rail tramway connected Miller's sawmill to the chute; Pritchard's 1969 survey found its remnant and a sandstone-lined cliff cut. On the 'earliest railroad' claim: sources located document the horse tramway but none support calling it one of California's first railroads — treat that claim as unverified.

ports.name: Fisk Mill Cove
ports.summary: John C. Fisk began lumbering and milling here in 1860; ownership passed to Frederick M. Helmke in 1865, who closed the mill in 1876, but the chute stayed active under the Kruse family, transhipping for other mills including Platt's mill 1.75 miles up the coast (at Horseshoe/Timber Gulch). The 1889 Coast Pilot: chute on the south point of the west side, vessel broadside in 14 ft with six mooring lines, four buoys; vessels to 100 tons; about 40 schooners loaded yearly with lumber, wood, bark and posts; 'quite a village' half a mile inside the point. A rare wood-and-iron capstan survives on the bluff.

ports.name: Stewarts Point
ports.summary: John and Andrew Fisk built the first landing in 1867; by 1877 three trough chutes served nearby mills, though by 1885 only the middle chute was operable (to 11 ft of water, seven mooring lines; vessels to 125 tons; ~25 schooners/yr with wood, posts, tanbark, shingles). H.A. Richardson bought the property in 1881, built his own chute, and the family shipped for ~40 years — a wire chute by the 1917 Coast Pilot, steam- and horse-drawn railroads to the cliff edge, and their own fleet of schooners and steam schooners — until trucks replaced water shipment in 1925. The settlement reached ~30 buildings and survives as an essentially unaltered doghole-port hamlet (Sonoma County Historic District).

ports.name: Bihler Landing (Black Point)
ports.summary: On the former German Rancho (Ernest Rufus grant, 1845), William Bihler ranched from the 1850s and turned to lumbering in the 1860s-70s; by 1875 Bihler and D.L.B. Ross built a landing with a slide chute, adding a second in 1876 (only the outer, reaching 23-ft water, was used; six mooring lines, three buoys). It shipped produce, tanbark, posts, firewood, staves and railroad ties — a summer-only landing averaging five small schooners a month (1889 Coast Pilot). A wire chute replaced the slide chutes around 1900; the Benders bought in 1904 and the port operated until 1917. The adjacent Black Point community had over a dozen buildings (hotel, store, post office, blacksmith, wagon shop, livery).

ports.name: Del Mar Landing
ports.summary: Charles Meyer and William Benitz established a produce/grain landing at a small cove here in 1849 (lost with the rancho, 1855). The lumber-era port dates from 1898, when brothers William and George Bender built a mill and wire chute just south, adding saloon, store and lumber warehouse by 1903; the mill burned in 1910 and the wire chute was likely abandoned soon after (the 1917 Coast Pilot still notes a wire cable; the 1929 T-sheet shows none). Tanbark and split stakes were among products shipped; the topography gave loading vessels no protection.

ports.name: Gualala
ports.summary: The Cole brothers built the first (apron) chute in 1865; C.D. Robinson bought it in 1866 and rebuilt it in 1875 as a cable chute with a donkey engine to haul the car back (Palmer 1880). The Gualala Mill Co. (Rutherford & Webber, spring 1862; later Harmon, Dingley & the Heywoods) sawed at the river mouth until the mill burned 14 September 1906; from the 1870s its lumber went by rail two miles north to Bourns Landing rather than over the exposed Gualala bluff chutes, which the 1889 Coast Pilot describes as two wire cable-chutes under the north bluff 'abandoned in 1884' (though the 1917 Coast Pilot again notes a wire chute). The mill company owned three schooners and ~12,000 acres of timber.

ports.name: Bourns Landing
ports.summary: Chief shipping point for the Gualala mill, 1.5 mi NW of the river. Franchise for wharf and chutes granted to Morton Bourn 22 February 1870; the Gualala Mill Co. added its own chute in 1872 (washed away 1878 by a southeaster, rebuilt 1879). The 1889 Coast Pilot describes a 200-ft northern chute reaching 24-ft water (lumber only), a southern chute (wood, bark, ties, posts, stave-bolts), a small cove inside with two small landing-wharves and a wharf served by a railroad branch, plus a new 'trapeze' wire-rope chute; ~140 cargoes shipped yearly, six 250-ton vessels at moorings in summer. Still listed as a working landing in the 1911 Coast & Geodetic Survey.

ports.name: Fish Rock (Havens Anchorage / Anchor Bay)
ports.summary: Cove sheltered by the twin Fish Rocks, named Havens Anchorage by the Coast Survey in 1853. State franchises: wharf to Mart T. Smith 13 May 1861; chute to E.J. The 1889 Coast Pilot: chute from the NE bluff point over 15 ft of water, vessel broadside with 5-6 mooring lines; wood, posts and ties shipped year-round; five or six vessels could shelter under the rocks in NW blows; 200-ton vessels could anchor close in.

ports.name: Iversen's Landing (Fergusons Cove / Rough and Ready)
ports.summary: Rock-choked cove under Iversen Point, 8¼ mi SE of Point Arena, protected somewhat by Saunders Reef. The 1889 Coast Pilot: a small platform chute on the north bank with a wire ('trapeze') carried across the cove; vessels of 100 tons lay stern-in 17 ft of water moored to the rocks; ~30 vessels/yr loaded wood, tanbark, posts and ties, fleeing to Havens Anchorage when SW swell came in. The Rough and Ready chute on Iversen Point itself washed away three times and was being re-erected in 1885. Namesake Niels Iversen (b. Denmark 1830) rebuilt the schooners Annie Iverson (1869) and Sina Johnson (1875) in the area.

ports.name: Greenwood (Elk)

ports.name: Mendocino (Big River)
ports.summary: Founded on the Frolic: the Baltimore-built opium brig wrecked at Point Cabrillo 25 July 1850; Henry Meiggs's salvage agent Jerome Ford found no cargo but reported the redwood, and Meiggs's brig Ontario landed mill machinery in July 1852 (California Lumber Co.; first mill on the point 1852, second on the river flats 1853-54; reorganized after Meiggs's 1854 failure, eventually the Mendocino Lumber Co.; mill burned 17 Oct 1863, rebuilt 1864, 55,000 ft/day both sides) — the origin story verified against Thomas Layton's Frolic research. ports.name: Fort Bragg (Soldiers Harbor)
ports.summary: The military post (est. 1857 to watch the reservation; abandoned by the mid-1860s — 'many years ago' per 1889 CP) gave its name to the cove C.R. ports.name: Cleone (Laguna Point)

ports.name: Newport
ports.summary: 'One of the most contracted anchorages on the coast' — a cove 150 by 60 yards. The Field Brothers' mill (2 mi east on Mill Creek, Ten Mile drainage) burned 1877; brothers-in-law Calvin Stewart and James Hunter rebuilt it in 1878 (25,000 ft/day) and hauled lumber by six-horse jerk-line teams to a 260-ft gravity chute reaching 18 ft of water; a 200-ton vessel could load amid an elaborate web of six-plus moorings — no spot on the coast demanded more shiphandling skill. ~50 vessels/yr. C.R. Johnson bought in 1882, concluded the port could never grow, and moved the mill to Fort Bragg in 1885; by 1887 only posts and ties were loaded, and the landing died.
ports.loading_method: single gravity/apron chute, 260 ft, to 18 ft water; extensive moorings; no wharf

ports.name: Kibesillah
ports.summary: Settled in the 1860s (first business, a blacksmith shop, 1867), Kibesillah grew to 20-30 buildings with three hotels and its own newspaper, shipping posts, cordwood and tanbark (not lumber, per Palmer) over its chute. The 1889 Coast Pilot describes a very substantial 90-yard wharf continued by an apron over 20 ft of water — but by 1885 no moorings were laid and the landing was 'practically abandoned,' vessels having no demand for ties there. When Stewart, Hunter and Johnson moved the mill to Fort Bragg in 1885 the town followed — hence 'the Mother of Fort Bragg.'

ports.name: Westport
ports.summary: First settled by Samuel Beal(l) (hence Beal's Landing); Fred Helmke's unfranchised 1875 chute soon washed away; James T. Rodgers built the wharf and chute in 1877 and renamed the town (Palmer 1880 says for Eastport, Maine; Wikipedia says Westport, Connecticut — unresolved). Palmer: a 375-ft wharf, 20 ft wide, with a ~200-ft suspension span, its outer end on a large rock, carrying two chutes. A new 610-ft chute with 75-ft apron (1882) let the loaded car haul the empty back. Two chutes (N and S) served three mills on Wages Creek plus DeHaven, Howard Creek and other feeders; ~65 vessels/yr, up to 85,000 ft loaded in a day; shipping suspended four months each winter, moorings lifted and overhauled. The south wharf was abandoned by 1900 and the port faded after WWI with the tie market.

ports.name: Howard Creek
ports.summary: Several small mills but no real town, north of Westport (Howards settled 1867; ranch farmhouse finished 1871). Mill ownership ran: Howard Creek Lumber Co. 1903-06, leased to Star Lumber Co. 1906-13, Duffy Brothers 1914-Nov 1915, Sexton Lumber Co. 1915-c.1920, restarted by Ira Thompson and burned 1924. In its last years a small railroad with a four-wheel truck hauled lumber to the wharf at Westport; MCMRHS doubts the 'narrow gauge' label, reading the photos as standard gauge with a Shay-type offset boiler.

ports.name: Union Landing
ports.summary: Busy shipping point without a mill of its own, serving many small mills nearby (incl. the Juan Creek timber). W.P. McFaul built the first wharf, shipping six-foot railroad ties to San Pedro for the Los Angeles Railway. After W.P. Frick acquired the Big Juan Creek timber in 1920, he had a new wharf built in 1926 — the last wharf ever built on the Mendocino coast — which the Depression left barely used. A large hotel/boarding house served the wharf hands.

ports.name: Hardy Creek
ports.summary: Mill settlement just around the point from Rockport; the mill was part of the Cottoneva Lumber Co. of Rockport and was operated by E.T. Dusenbury, one of its owners. It had its own wharf and a railroad, and the town a large hotel; the mill burned and was never rebuilt. The 1889 Coast Pilot already names Hardy's Rock on this shore; the mill era therefore falls in the Cottoneva Lumber Co. period (c.1886-1900s) but exact years are unverified.

ports.name: Rockport (Cottoneva Cove)
alt_names: Miles' Chute (local name of the chute)
ports.summary: William R. Miller landed mill machinery from the schooner David and Edward in October 1876 and built the first sawmill; the wharf-and-chute complex of 1876 cost $14,000 and was called the finest on the Mendocino coast (Palmer: 275-ft suspension span with seven cables a side). The 1889 Coast Pilot describes the mature system: a 175-yard wire suspension bridge from the north point to a 50-ft rock, a tramway across the rock, and a 45-yard chute over 15 ft of water; four principal mooring buoys; mill (25,000 ft/day) 1/3 mi up Cottoneva Creek, lumber brought by tramway, logs by steam railway; ~24 cargoes/yr; landing unused about four months after 1 December. Ownership: Miller to Cottoneva Lumber Co. 1886 (mill burned 1900); New York & Pennsylvania (Redwood) Co. c.1907 built a new mill (also burned); Cottoneva Lumber Co. reincorporated 1910 (nothing built); Finkbine-Guild Lumber Co. 1925-27 (financial disaster); Southern Redwood Co. 1928-29; Rockport Redwood Co. chartered under Dusenbury interests in the 1930s (trucking era).
ports.active_years: 1876-1929 (sea shipping); mill revivals to 1950s by truck
ports.loading_method: suspension bridge + island tramway + trough chute (15 ft water); largest 'anchorage... large in comparison with Westport, Kibesillah, Newport' (1889 CP)

ports.railroad: tramway along the gulch at +52 ft to the bridge; steam log railway up Cottoneva Valley (1880s); Finkbine-Guild standard logging RR (1920s, gauge unverified)

ports.name: Usal
ports.summary: In 1880 Palmer found only two or three buildings and a telegraph line; the industrial town came in 1889, when a mill, wharf and company town were built at the Usal Creek mouth with a railroad running about three miles up the creek — Wikipedia's Lost Coast article credits Robert Dollar with building it in 1889, while other accounts have Dollar acquiring the works in 1894 (his steamer Newsboy served the port); flag this discrepancy. The mill was destroyed by fire in 1902 (with schoolhouse, warehouse and the county bridge), the railroad was dismantled (its Shay No. 1 sold to Glen Blair in 1903), and the surviving hotel burned in 1969. Palmer's 'Northport,' 16 miles north of Cottoneva with a steam-powered cable-and-cage instead of a chute (Funk & Co., resident partner Walter Fisk), lay in this vicinity — its precise relation to Usal is unresolved.
